The FY25 bridge sets the base. Productivity covered only 37% of the $1,101m of gross pressure. The cost to income ratio ex Notable Items went from 50.3% to 53.0%.

The FY26 pressures are large. The EBA increase is 3% to 4% on a $6,326m staff expense base, plus a superannuation increase. About 610 announced front line bankers (~350 Business, ~80 WIB, ~180 Consumer) were only c.40% to c.60% onboarded at Sep-25, so a full year cost still arrives. UNITE spend rises to $850m-$950m at ~75% expensed, which is roughly $638m-$713m through the P&L against roughly $488m-$502m in FY25 (our arithmetic on the disclosed 74%-76% expensed share of $660m). Amortisation rose $106m to $995m in FY25 and its FY26 growth is guided only to 'moderate', not to stop.

What actually creates positive jaws in FY26 sits outside productivity. The $273m Fit for Growth charge is 2.3% of the FY25 expense base, so its non-repeat alone lowers FY26 reported expense growth by that amount. # CBA: FY25 → FY26 earnings-engine rotation

## Group P&L, cash basis, continuing operations ($M)

| Line | FY24 | FY25 | FY25 vs FY24 | FY26 | FY26 vs FY25 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Net interest income | 22,824 | 24,023 | +5% | 25,586 | +7% |
| Other operating income | 4,350 | 4,442 | +2% | 4,638 | +4% |
| Total operating income | 27,174 | 28,465 | +5% | 30,224 | +6% |
| Operating expenses | (12,218) | (12,996) | +6% | (13,755) | +6% |
| **Pre-provision profit** | 14,956 | 15,469 | **+3%** | 16,469 | **+6%** |
| Loan impairment expense | (802) | (726) | −9% | (788) | +9% |
| Cash NPAT | 9,836 | 10,252 | **+4%** | 10,982 | **+7%** |
| NIM | 1.99% | 2.08% | +9bps | 2.05% | −3bps |
| Loan loss rate (LIE/GLAA) | n/a | 0.07% | — | 0.08% | +1bp |

*Sources: CBA-FY26-profit-announcement p.16; CBA-FY25-profit-announcement p.16, p.18.*

## The rotation

FY25's cash-NPAT growth (+4%) was margin- and provision-led: NIM rose 9bps, mostly from replicating-portfolio and capital-hedge earnings (+9bps) and a liquids mix benefit (+7bps), while opex (+6%) outgrew income (+5%), holding pre-provision profit growth to +3%. The bottom line was then flattered by a shrinking impairment charge (−9%, "reflecting an improving base case economic outlook and lower loss experience").

FY26 rotates to a volume-led model. Average interest-earning assets rose 8% ($92bn), lifting NII +7% even as NIM fell 3bps to 2.05%. CBA's margin bridge (results presentation p.60) attributes the fall to Liquids & repos (−4bps) and Asset pricing (−5bps: home loan competition −3bps, cash-rate lag −1bp, business/institutional lending −1bp), partly offset by hedge income (+5bps) and Portfolio mix (+2bps, "deposits growing faster than lending"). Opex grew +6%, matching income, so pre-provision profit growth doubled to +6% and cost-to-income improved 20bps to 45.5%. Loan impairment expense rose +9% (loss rate 7bps→8bps) on "portfolio growth, cost-of-living pressures and increased geopolitical risk" — provisioning for risk, not realised losses, which the ASX announcement states "remained low," with provision coverage steady at 1.53% of credit RWA and the loss rate still below its 17-year historical range (results presentation p.69).

## Judgment

On the disclosed evidence, FY26's faster cash-NPAT growth (+7% vs +4%) is higher quality. It is broader-based (income growth matched cost growth for the first time in this comparison, doubling pre-provision profit growth to +6%) and it absorbed, rather than depended on, both NIM compression and a rising loan-loss rate — whereas FY25's growth relied on non-repeatable margin tailwinds and a shrinking impairment charge while pre-provision profit growth lagged at +3%.

## Limitations

- No published dollar bridge decomposes cash-NPAT growth into volume/margin/cost/impairment/tax; this judgment is inferred from growth-rate comparisons and the bps-level NIM bridge.
- Other operating income includes unquantified one-off items (CommInsure milestone payment, Gemini IPO gain), so "clean" organic OOI growth cannot be isolated.
- The higher loan-loss rate is expected-loss provisioning; documents assert realised losses "remained low" but disclose no write-off rate to verify this.

**Confidence: 78/100**


Key facts:
- FY26 cash NPAT rose 7% to $10,982m (from $10,252m), a faster pace than FY25's 4% growth to $10,252m (from $9,836m).
- The margin trend reversed: NIM rose 9bps to 2.08% in FY25 but fell 3bps to 2.05% in FY26.
- FY26 loan impairment expense rose 9% to $788m and the loan loss rate ticked up 1bp to 8bps of GLAA, versus a 9% decline to $726m (loss rate 7bps) in FY25.
- Pre-provision profit growth doubled from +3% in FY25 (income +5%, opex +6%) to +6% in FY26 (income +6%, opex +6%), showing FY26 income growth caught up to cost growth.
- CBA's FY26 margin bridge attributes the 3bp NIM decline mainly to asset pricing competition (-5bps: home loan competition -3bps, cash rate lag -1bp, business/institutional lending -1bp).
- The FY26 margin bridge shows hedge/replicating income continuing to offset pricing pressure: Capital, Replicating and Other added 5bps (replicating portfolio +4bps, capital hedges +1bp), similar in direction to FY25's larger 9bp tailwind from the same source.
- Growth in liquid assets and institutional repos cost the FY26 margin 4bps combined, a bridge item that did not appear in FY25 (where liquids/pooled facilities instead added 7bps).
- FY26 net interest income grew 7% to $25,586m, driven by an 8% ($92bn) rise in average interest-earning assets that outweighed the 3bp NIM decline.
- FY26's higher loan-loss rate reflects provisioning for risk rather than realised losses: CBA states realised credit losses remained low and provision coverage stayed strong, with the loss rate still below its historical range.
- Restructuring and notable items excluded from underlying opex have risen each year ($89m FY24, $130m FY25, $170m FY26), a modest but growing drag embedded in both years' headline cost growth.
- Part of FY26's other operating income growth (+4% to $4,638m) came from non-recurring items, including a fair value gain on the Gemini IPO investment, which are not separately quantified in the disclosure.

Verdict: normalisation is real but not complete. The low FY25 impairment charge ($424m, 5bps of average loans, down from $537m/7bps in FY24) is genuinely earned: stressed exposures to TCE fell to 1.28% from 1.45%, mortgage 90+ delinquencies fell to 0.70% from 1.05%, and other consumer 90+ delinquencies fell to 1.08% from 1.40%. # FY25 earnings conversion: CBA best, then NAB, then Westpac

**Judgment.** CBA converted best. It is the only one of the three whose preferred measure
grew at all, and it leads on both steps of the conversion chain. Westpac lost the result at
the cost line. NAB lost it below the pre-provision line.

## The chain, on each bank's own preferred basis, FY25 v FY24

| Line | CBA cash, FY to Jun-25 [1] | NAB cash, FY to Sep-25 [5] | WBC ex-Notables, FY to Sep-25 [9] |

Two gaps, from my arithmetic on those printed lines. Income growth less expense growth: CBA
-1.6pp, NAB -1.8pp, WBC -5.7pp. Pre-provision growth to earnings growth: CBA +0.8pp, WBC
+0.5pp, NAB -1.5pp. CBA leads both steps. Second place turns on which step you weight.

## Drivers

**CBA.** Expenses (+6%) outran income (+5%), so operating performance rose only 3%. A $76m
fall in loan impairment expense then lifted cash NPAT to +4% [3]. Its income was also the
most core: NIM +9bps to 2.08%, +2bps after liquid assets and pooled facilities [2][4].

**Westpac.** Expenses rose 9%, and still 6% without a $273m Fit for Growth restructuring
charge that Westpac did not classify as a Notable Item [10][11]. Pre-provision profit fell
3%; adding the charge back leaves it flat, my arithmetic, not a disclosed line. The largest
credit tailwind of the three, 5bps of average loans against 7bps, recovered only half a point
[9][11]. Core NIM slipped 1bp to 1.81% [12].

**NAB.** NAB had the tightest cost growth, +4.6%, or +3.2% without $130m of payroll review
and remediation cost, and delivered +1.3% underlying profit [6]. It was then the only bank
with a rising credit charge, $833m or +14.4%, from individually assessed charges in Corporate
and Institutional Banking [7], plus non-controlling interests of $39m against $18m [5]. Its

- Different periods. CBA's year ends 30 June 2025, NAB's and Westpac's on 30 September 2025.

  also excludes disposal, closure and demerger results, $137m [2]. NAB also excludes
  amortisation of acquired intangibles, $303m, of which $295m is acquisitions and disposals
  [5][14][15]. NAB's bar is the lowest to clear and Westpac's the highest.
- One-off costs stay inside all three pre-provision lines, $273m at WBC and $130m at each of

- Statutory profit ranks them differently: CBA +8%, WBC -1%, NAB -2.9% [1][9][5], so NAB and
  Westpac swap. I prefer the preferred-measure comparison, because the question is each bank's
  own conversion chain, but the swap shows the ordering depends on adjustment scope. CBA's two
  bases disagree on its own pre-provision step: +5% statutory against +3% cash [1].
- The documents give no normalised credit charge and no mix-adjusted comparison, so the credit
  swings cannot be separated from portfolio quality.

CBA FY25 to FY26: the engine rotated from price to volume, and from provision release to provision build. Verdict: yes, FY26 is the higher-quality year, but only because hedge earnings paid for the customer-price loss.

1. THE ROTATION. FY25 was a price year with almost no balance sheet: net interest income rose 5% on a 9 basis point margin lift and only $9 billion of average interest earning assets. FY26 is the mirror image: net interest income rose 7% on $92 billion (+8%) of average interest earning assets while margin fell 3 basis points. On the cash, continuing-operations basis, operating income moved from +5% ($28,465m) to +6.2% ($30,224m); underlying operating expenses from +6% ($12,866m) to +5.6% ($13,585m); pre-provision profit from +3% ($15,469m) to +6.5% ($16,469m); loan impairment expense from $726m (-9%) to $788m (+9%); cash NPAT from +4% ($10,252m) to +7.1% ($10,982m). Cost-to-income moved from 45.7% (+70bps) to 45.5% (-20bps). Cash ROE moved from 13.5% (-10bps) to 14.0% (+50bps). Profit after capital charge moved from $5,839m (+5%) to $6,464m (+11%).

Arithmetic on the disclosed lines: FY25's $589m pre-tax uplift was $513m of operating performance plus $76m of impairment relief (13% of the uplift). FY26's $938m pre-tax uplift was $1,000m of operating performance less $62m of impairment. FY25 bought its 4% with negative jaws and a provision release. FY26 earned 7% with positive jaws while paying more for credit. ROE and the risk-adjusted PACC measure confirm the direction: FY25 grew profit while ROE fell 10 basis points; FY26 lifted ROE 50 basis points and PACC 11%.

2. THE MARGIN BRIDGE. CBA prints two versions of the same 208 to 205 basis point walk. The profit announcement (p.28) shows: liquids (3), asset pricing (5), funding costs flat, portfolio mix +2, basis risk flat, capital/replicating/other +5, Treasury and Markets (2). The results presentation (slide 60) shows: liquids and repos (4) (liquid assets 3, institutional repos 1), asset pricing (5) (home loan competition 3, cash rate lag 1, business and institutional lending 1), funding costs flat, portfolio mix +2, interest rate risk hedging +5 (replicating portfolio 4, capital 1), Treasury and Markets (1). They differ only in where the roughly 1 basis point institutional-repo drag sits. I prefer the presentation version because it isolates the full 4 basis points of drag from balance-sheet items CBA itself labels as having minimal impact on earnings. On that rebasing, underlying margin rose 1 basis point, from 2.04% to 2.05%. So the reported compression is a mix effect from +$15bn of average liquid assets and +$11bn of average institutional repos, not customer-margin erosion. But the underlying margin only held flat because +5 basis points of replicating-portfolio and capital-hedge earnings exactly cancelled -5 basis points of lending price competition. That is a swap-rate outcome, not a franchise outcome.

3. THE LOSS RATE IS A BUILD, NOT A BLEED. The 8 basis point loan loss rate (from 7 basis points) sits against improving stock metrics: gross non-performing exposures fell to 0.69% of total committed exposures from 0.73%, and net write-offs rose only 1 basis point to 0.07% of average gross loans. FY25 was the opposite: the charge fell 2 basis points while non-performing exposures rose 14%. CBA increased the Downside scenario weighting during FY26 with a commensurate decrease in the Central scenario, and individually assessed provisions fell 3% to $791m. This is forward-looking provisioning, not realised deterioration.

4. WHAT THE DISCLOSURE DOES NOT SUPPORT. Coverage was consumed, not added: total provisions rose only 2% to $6,476m against 6% credit risk-weighted asset growth, so total provisions to credit RWA fell 7 basis points to 1.53%. The $788m charge did not keep pace with the book, so describing coverage as strong is fair on level but not on direction. The second half broke the trend: 2H26 impairment was $469m, up 47% on 1H26 and 9 basis points annualised; home loan 90+ day arrears reached 0.73% (+10bps on the half) and personal loan arrears 1.72% (+31bps). Two non-operating items helped: other operating income (+$196m) includes an unquantified CommInsure General Insurance milestone payment and a Gemini IPO fair-value gain, and the effective tax rate fell 50 basis points to 30.0%, worth roughly $80m on the arithmetic, about a tenth of the $730m uplift. Growth is narrow and capital-hungry: Business Banking (+11%) and Retail Banking Services (+5%) carried the year while New Zealand fell 7% and Institutional Banking and Markets grew 2%; CET1 fell 30 basis points to 12.0% with 72 basis points of capital deployed into credit risk-weighted assets.

CONCLUSION. FY26 is genuinely higher quality. The growth came from pre-provision profit rather than the provision line, jaws turned positive, ROE and risk-adjusted profit improved, and the margin optics are a liquids and repo artefact rather than franchise damage. Two qualifications keep it from being a clean win: the underlying margin was held flat by interest-rate hedges rather than pricing power, and provision coverage thinned to fund volume growth.

- FY26 cash NPAT from continuing operations rose $730 million or 7% to $10,982 million, driven by 6% operating income growth, 6% operating expense growth and a $62 million INCREASE in loan impairment expense.

# NAB FY25: Was B&PB growth value-accretive?

**Verdict: Yes, on balance.** Growth was broad-based, deposit-funded, and held returns per unit of risk flat — but it was not free: 8bps of NIM went to competition and deposit mix, jaws were slightly negative, and the NPL stock rose materially. The credit deterioration sits in the stock, not the FY25 charge, and the 2H25 impaired spike is substantially two Agri single names.

| B&PB (restated) | FY25 | FY24 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| GLAs | $279.5bn | $261.7bn | +6.8% |
| — Business lending | $166.3bn | $155.0bn | +7.3% |
| Net operating income | $8,531m | $8,358m | +2.1% |
| Cash earnings | $3,330m | $3,277m | +1.6% |
| NIM | 3.01% | 3.09% | −8bps |
| CIC / GLAs | 0.19% | 0.20% | −1bp |
| Cash earnings / avg RWA | 2.18% | 2.19% | −1bp |
| Cost to income | 37.9% | 37.6% | +30bps |
| Impaired / GLAs | 0.49% | 0.39% | +10bps |
| Default-not-impaired / GLAs | 2.05% | 1.74% | +31bps |

(Results book, PDF p.36)

**Reconciliation.** Volume did the work: average interest-earning assets +5.4% converted to NII of only +2.8% because NIM gave up 8bps to "competitive pressures impacting both the business and housing lending portfolios, as well as higher deposit costs" (results book p.37). The margin stabilised in 2H25 (3.01%→3.02%). Other income fell 2.9% (of which $22m was the NZ wealth disposal). Costs +2.9% (bankers, technology) left underlying profit +1.6%; the CIC rose only $6m, so cash earnings also grew 1.6%. Deposits +6.6% to $237.9bn broadly funded the $17.8bn of lending growth.

**Margin vs credit as the price of growth.** The P&L credit cost did not rise with volume: CIC/GLAs fell 1bp to 0.19%, and the business-lending charge fell YoY ($209m+$308m halves in FY24 vs $165m+$266m in FY25 — presentation p.95); the FY25 increase was housing. The stock deteriorated: B&PB NPEs reached $7,079m, 2.54% of GLAs (2.12% Sep 24), and business-lending NPLs 3.22% of business GLAs (2.66%). RWA grew 9.0% — faster than GLAs — partly from "deterioration in asset quality", yet cash earnings/avg RWA held at 2.18% and combined Business Banking ROE is disclosed at 18%.

**Broad-based vs single-name.** Growth: broad-based — "business lending across a broad range of sectors" (results book p.24); Agri +3.5%, Health +5.9%, CRE +7.4%, Other +10.4%, small business +9.2%; SME share up to 28.0% (presentation p.50). Deterioration: the FY-long default-not-impaired build (+31bps) is portfolio-wide, but the Sep-25 impaired spike is single-name-skewed — two large, well-secured Agri customers add 21bps to the 3.22% NPL ratio, excluding which the ratio fell 3bps HoH to 3.01%; watch loans fell 9bps, the first decline since Mar 23 (presentation p.26-27). Underwriting looks held: 73% fully secured, 6% unsecured, sub-investment-grade share 77% vs 78% (presentation p.95).

**Net:** value-accretive growth at broadly flat risk-adjusted returns, with modest margin/cost dilution — not growth bought with credit standards.

Confidence: 80/100.


Key facts:
- B&PB gross loans and acceptances grew 6.8% to $279.5bn in FY25, with business lending up 7.3% to $166.3bn and housing up 5.8% to $109.3bn.
- B&PB net operating income rose 2.1% to $8,531m and cash earnings rose 1.6% to $3,330m, so revenue and earnings grew far slower than volumes.
- B&PB NIM fell 8bps to 3.01% in FY25 due to lending competition and deposit costs, but rose 1bp half-on-half in 2H25.
- B&PB average interest earning assets rose 5.4% ($12.8bn), converting to net interest income growth of only 2.8% ($204m) after the margin decline.
- The B&PB credit impairment charge rose only $6m (1.1%) to $529m, and CIC to GLAs fell 1bp to 0.19%; the increase was housing-driven, with business lending charges lower year on year.
- By half, B&PB business-lending impairment charges were $209m/$308m in FY24 versus $165m/$266m in FY25, while housing charges swung from write-backs to $37m/$16m.
- B&PB asset-quality stock metrics deteriorated over FY25: impaired assets to GLAs +10bps to 0.49% and default-but-not-impaired +31bps to 2.05%.
- B&PB non-performing exposures rose to $7,079m or 2.54% of GLAs at Sep 25 from $5,580m or 2.12% at Sep 24; business-lending NPLs reached 3.22% of business GLAs versus 2.66%.
- The Sep-25 spike in the B&PB business-lending NPL ratio is substantially two single names: two large well-secured Agri customers account for 21bps, and excluding them the ratio fell 3bps half-on-half to 3.01%.
- The half-on-half rise in default-but-not-impaired assets was driven by a small number of large Agriculture downgrades in B&PB, and group-wide single names sat in C&IB and NZ Banking.
- Lending growth was broad-based, not concentrated: business lending grew across a broad range of sectors, with Agri +3.5%, Health +5.9%, CRE +7.4%, Other +10.4% and small business +9.2%, and SME market share rose to 28.0%.
- Underwriting settings look held rather than loosened: the business book stayed 73% fully secured and 6% unsecured, and the sub-investment-grade-equivalent share edged down to 77% from 78%.
- Group watch loans fell 9bps to 1.17% of GLAs in 2H25, the first half-yearly reduction since Mar 23, supporting a stabilising underlying credit trend.
- Growth consumed capital faster than it earned: B&PB RWA rose 9.0% ($13.2bn), partly from asset-quality deterioration, yet cash earnings on average RWA held at 2.18% (down 1bp) and cash earnings on average assets fell 5bps to 1.25%.
- Growth was largely self-funded and jaws slightly negative: customer deposits grew 6.6% to $237.9bn, operating expenses rose 2.9% and the cost to income ratio rose 30bps to 37.9%.
- Combined Business Banking (B&PB plus C&IB) is disclosed at an 18% FY25 ROE on stated assumptions, supporting returns-accretive growth at the business-bank level.
- Group collective provisions for the B&PB business book rose for both volume growth and asset-quality deterioration, and individually assessed provisions were raised for the B&PB business lending portfolio.

# CBA: FY25 → FY26 earnings-engine rotation

## Group P&L, cash basis, continuing operations ($M)

| Line | FY24 | FY25 | FY25 vs FY24 | FY26 | FY26 vs FY25 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Net interest income | 22,824 | 24,023 | +5% | 25,586 | +7% |
| Other operating income | 4,350 | 4,442 | +2% | 4,638 | +4% |
| Total operating income | 27,174 | 28,465 | +5% | 30,224 | +6% |
| Operating expenses | (12,218) | (12,996) | +6% | (13,755) | +6% |
| **Pre-provision profit** | 14,956 | 15,469 | **+3%** | 16,469 | **+6%** |
| Loan impairment expense | (802) | (726) | −9% | (788) | +9% |
| Cash NPAT | 9,836 | 10,252 | **+4%** | 10,982 | **+7%** |
| NIM | 1.99% | 2.08% | +9bps | 2.05% | −3bps |
| Loan loss rate (LIE/GLAA) | n/a | 0.07% | — | 0.08% | +1bp |

*Sources: CBA-FY26-profit-announcement p.16; CBA-FY25-profit-announcement p.16, p.18.*

## The rotation

FY25's cash-NPAT growth (+4%) was margin- and provision-led: NIM rose 9bps, mostly from replicating-portfolio and capital-hedge earnings (+9bps) and a liquids mix benefit (+7bps), while opex (+6%) outgrew income (+5%), holding pre-provision profit growth to +3%. The bottom line was then flattered by a shrinking impairment charge (−9%, "reflecting an improving base case economic outlook and lower loss experience").

FY26 rotates to a volume-led model. Average interest-earning assets rose 8% ($92bn), lifting NII +7% even as NIM fell 3bps to 2.05%. CBA's margin bridge (results presentation p.60) attributes the fall to Liquids & repos (−4bps) and Asset pricing (−5bps: home loan competition −3bps, cash-rate lag −1bp, business/institutional lending −1bp), partly offset by hedge income (+5bps) and Portfolio mix (+2bps, "deposits growing faster than lending"). Opex grew +6%, matching income, so pre-provision profit growth doubled to +6% and cost-to-income improved 20bps to 45.5%. Loan impairment expense rose +9% (loss rate 7bps→8bps) on "portfolio growth, cost-of-living pressures and increased geopolitical risk" — provisioning for risk, not realised losses, which the ASX announcement states "remained low," with provision coverage steady at 1.53% of credit RWA and the loss rate still below its 17-year historical range (results presentation p.69).

## Judgment

On the disclosed evidence, FY26's faster cash-NPAT growth (+7% vs +4%) is higher quality. It is broader-based (income growth matched cost growth for the first time in this comparison, doubling pre-provision profit growth to +6%) and it absorbed, rather than depended on, both NIM compression and a rising loan-loss rate — whereas FY25's growth relied on non-repeatable margin tailwinds and a shrinking impairment charge while pre-provision profit growth lagged at +3%.

## Limitations

- No published dollar bridge decomposes cash-NPAT growth into volume/margin/cost/impairment/tax; this judgment is inferred from growth-rate comparisons and the bps-level NIM bridge.
- Other operating income includes unquantified one-off items (CommInsure milestone payment, Gemini IPO gain), so "clean" organic OOI growth cannot be isolated.
- The higher loan-loss rate is expected-loss provisioning; documents assert realised losses "remained low" but disclose no write-off rate to verify this.

**Confidence: 78/100**


Key facts:
- FY26 cash NPAT rose 7% to $10,982m (from $10,252m), a faster pace than FY25's 4% growth to $10,252m (from $9,836m).
- The margin trend reversed: NIM rose 9bps to 2.08% in FY25 but fell 3bps to 2.05% in FY26.
- FY26 loan impairment expense rose 9% to $788m and the loan loss rate ticked up 1bp to 8bps of GLAA, versus a 9% decline to $726m (loss rate 7bps) in FY25.
- Pre-provision profit growth doubled from +3% in FY25 (income +5%, opex +6%) to +6% in FY26 (income +6%, opex +6%), showing FY26 income growth caught up to cost growth.
- CBA's FY26 margin bridge attributes the 3bp NIM decline mainly to asset pricing competition (-5bps: home loan competition -3bps, cash rate lag -1bp, business/institutional lending -1bp).
- The FY26 margin bridge shows hedge/replicating income continuing to offset pricing pressure: Capital, Replicating and Other added 5bps (replicating portfolio +4bps, capital hedges +1bp), similar in direction to FY25's larger 9bp tailwind from the same source.
- Growth in liquid assets and institutional repos cost the FY26 margin 4bps combined, a bridge item that did not appear in FY25 (where liquids/pooled facilities instead added 7bps).
- FY26 net interest income grew 7% to $25,586m, driven by an 8% ($92bn) rise in average interest-earning assets that outweighed the 3bp NIM decline.
- FY26's higher loan-loss rate reflects provisioning for risk rather than realised losses: CBA states realised credit losses remained low and provision coverage stayed strong, with the loss rate still below its historical range.
- Restructuring and notable items excluded from underlying opex have risen each year ($89m FY24, $130m FY25, $170m FY26), a modest but growing drag embedded in both years' headline cost growth.
- Part of FY26's other operating income growth (+4% to $4,638m) came from non-recurring items, including a fair value gain on the Gemini IPO investment, which are not separately quantified in the disclosure.

# FY25 earnings conversion: CBA best, then NAB, then Westpac

**Judgment.** CBA converted best. It is the only one of the three whose preferred measure
grew at all, and it leads on both steps of the conversion chain. Westpac lost the result at
the cost line. NAB lost it below the pre-provision line.

## The chain, on each bank's own preferred basis, FY25 v FY24

| Line | CBA cash, FY to Jun-25 [1] | NAB cash, FY to Sep-25 [5] | WBC ex-Notables, FY to Sep-25 [9] |
|---|---|---|---|
| Operating income | 28,465, +5% | 20,813, +2.9% | 22,464, +3% |
| Operating expenses | (12,996), +6% | (9,848), +4.6% | (11,916), +9% |
| Pre-provision line | 15,469, +3% | 10,965, +1.3% | 10,548, (3%) |
| Impairment | (726), (9%) | (833), +14.4% | (424), (21%) |
| Preferred earnings | 10,252, +4% | 7,091, (0.2%) | 6,972, (2%) |
| Cost-income ratio | 45.7% from 45.0% [4] | 47.3% from 46.5% [8] | 53.0% from 50.3% [10] |

Two gaps, from my arithmetic on those printed lines. Income growth less expense growth: CBA
-1.6pp, NAB -1.8pp, WBC -5.7pp. Pre-provision growth to earnings growth: CBA +0.8pp, WBC
+0.5pp, NAB -1.5pp. CBA leads both steps. Second place turns on which step you weight.

## Drivers

**CBA.** Expenses (+6%) outran income (+5%), so operating performance rose only 3%. A $76m
fall in loan impairment expense then lifted cash NPAT to +4% [3]. Its income was also the
most core: NIM +9bps to 2.08%, +2bps after liquid assets and pooled facilities [2][4].

**Westpac.** Expenses rose 9%, and still 6% without a $273m Fit for Growth restructuring
charge that Westpac did not classify as a Notable Item [10][11]. Pre-provision profit fell
3%; adding the charge back leaves it flat, my arithmetic, not a disclosed line. The largest
credit tailwind of the three, 5bps of average loans against 7bps, recovered only half a point
[9][11]. Core NIM slipped 1bp to 1.81% [12].

**NAB.** NAB had the tightest cost growth, +4.6%, or +3.2% without $130m of payroll review
and remediation cost, and delivered +1.3% underlying profit [6]. It was then the only bank
with a rising credit charge, $833m or +14.4%, from individually assessed charges in Corporate
and Institutional Banking [7], plus non-controlling interests of $39m against $18m [5]. Its

- Different periods. CBA's year ends 30 June 2025, NAB's and Westpac's on 30 September 2025.
  No document restates to a common period.
- Different adjustment scope. Westpac excludes only hedging items, $56m after tax [13]. CBA

  amortisation of acquired intangibles, $303m, of which $295m is acquisitions and disposals

- Statutory profit ranks them differently: CBA +8%, WBC -1%, NAB -2.9% [1][9][5], so NAB and

  own conversion chain, but the swap shows the ordering depends on adjustment scope. CBA's two
  bases disagree on its own pre-provision step: +5% statutory against +3% cash [1].
- The documents give no normalised credit charge and no mix-adjusted comparison, so the credit
  swings cannot be separated from portfolio quality.

Judgment: the >$500m FY26 productivity target is sized as an offset to wage, banker and UNITE pressure, not as a jaws-restorer; the disclosure gives no FY26 revenue guidance, so positive jaws cannot be demonstrated from these documents. The investment mix pivoted to UNITE ($147m to $660m) from risk & regulatory ($1,059m to $695m), lifting the expensed share from 56% to 60% of a $1,918m total. For FY26 Westpac flags ~$2bn total investment, UNITE of $850-950m at ~75% expensed, reductions in the other two categories, a moderating (but still positive) amortisation increase, an EBA increase of 3-4% and continued banker investment. Westpac itself frames closing its CTI gap to peers (3.7ppts above at 1H25) as a Sep-29 outcome via UNITE. Productivity is mainly the funding mechanism that keeps ex-charge expense growth from re-running FY25's 6% while UNITE spend peaks; restoring positive jaws would require income growth above FY25's 3%, on which these documents are silent.
